The second write simply overwrites the first one, so the final value only reflects the last change instead of the combined effect. It is a classic read-modify-write race condition that occurs whenever multiple sessions operate on the same data without coordination. To prevent it pessimistically, you can use a row-level lock such as SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which forces the second reader to wait until the first transaction commits or rolls back before it can read the row. This guarantees that only one transaction at a time performs the modify-and-write sequence, eliminating the race entirely, though it does introduce waiting time and can reduce overall throughput under high contention. On the optimistic side, you can check a version stamp or checksum before committing; if the row has changed since you read it, the update fails and you retry the whole read-modify-write cycle. This approach avoids holding locks for the whole duration, so concurrency is higher, but it adds the overhead of retries when conflicts do occur and requires application logic to handle the retry loop gracefully.

Deadlocks happen when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs and neither can proceed, which creates a cycle in the wait-for graph. For example, transaction A updates row one then tries to lock row two, while transaction B updates row two then tries to lock row one. The database detects this cycle and aborts one transaction as the victim, releasing its locks so the other can complete. The single most effective application-side change is to always acquire rows in a consistent global order. If every transaction locks rows sorted by primary key, a cycle becomes impossible because the lock acquisition graph can never close. This eliminates deadlocks at the source rather than relying on detection and rollback. The trade-off is that you must know your access patterns upfront and may occasionally lock rows you don't immediately need, but in practice the consistency gain far outweighs the minor overhead. I'm unsure whether this holds perfectly under serializable isolation with predicate locking, since the wait-for graph can become more complex there, but for read-committed or repeatable-read with explicit row locks the approach is reliably effective.

Once a cycle is found, the database aborts one of the transactions as the victim and releases its locks, allowing the other transaction to complete. This ordering rule is simple to enforce and eliminates the root cause without needing to shrink transaction scope or rely on timeouts.

In a relational database deadlock happens when two separate transactions each hold a lock on a resource that the other one is trying to acquire. So transaction A might lock row one and then wait for row two, while transaction B has already locked row two and is now waiting for row one. Neither one can move forward because each is holding something the other needs, and that creates a cycle in the wait-for graph that the system has to resolve. The database will notice that cycle and then pick one of the transactions to roll back as the victim, releasing its locks so the other can complete. To prevent most of these from happening on the application side the single most effective change is to keep transactions as short as possible and make sure you are only touching the rows you actually need at that moment, which shrinks the window where a cycle can form. Of course there are other patterns but keeping the scope tight is what stops the majority of cases in practice.

The third reason is stale planner statistics; if the correlation column hasn't been updated after a large bulk load, the planner underestimates how many rows match the predicate and decides a sequential scan is cheaper. I'm not sure whether the issue is more likely the selectivity miscalculation or the stale stats, since both can produce similar estimated row counts, but I'd start with explain analyze and then run analyze if the numbers look off.

I start by saying that read committed is the default for most databases and that each statement in a transaction begins a fresh read of the committed data. So if transaction one reads a row, commits, and then transaction two updates and commits that same row, the next read in transaction one will see the new value. That is the non-repeatable read anomaly. Now repeatable read takes a single snapshot at the first read and holds it for the whole transaction. So if transaction one reads a row, and then transaction two inserts or updates a new row that transaction one hasn't seen yet, a second read of the same query will return the same rows as before, even if new committed rows exist. The anomaly that can still happen under repeatable read is a phantom read, where the set of rows changes between reads because of inserts. For a web application I would default to read committed because most requests are short-lived and reason about a single read, and the cost of maintaining a transaction snapshot across multiple requests is too high. I would choose repeatable read only when a single transaction needs to reason across multiple reads of the same data, like a money transfer that reads a balance and then updates it, and I would accept the phantom read risk or use range locks if I needed strict consistency. The trade-off is between consistency and throughput, and for typical request-response web workloads read committed gives enough correctness without the overhead.

An inner join only returns rows where both sides match the predicate, so if the left side has no match, the row disappears entirely. A left join guarantees every left row appears in the result, padding the right columns with NULL when there's no match. That padding is the key: a comparison against NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not true, so any condition written in the WHERE clause that references the right table will filter out those padded rows, effectively turning the join into an inner join. The join predicate belongs in the ON clause, where it controls which rows are combined before the outer join's null-padding happens. Conditions that describe the final result set, like filtering for a specific attribute on the right side, belong in WHERE. A practical symptom I've seen is missing rows in a report - when a developer adds a WHERE condition on the right table, rows that should appear vanish because the UNKNOWN comparison drops them. I would choose a left join when I need to preserve all records from the primary table, such as a user list with optional profile data, and use ON for the matching logic, moving any selective filters to WHERE to keep the join semantics intact.

ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. Atomicity means that every transaction is a single unit of work - either all the statements inside it execute and commit, or if any one fails, the whole thing rolls back and nothing changes. I think of it like a light switch: it's either on or off, never halfway. Consistency ensures that a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting all defined rules, constraints, and triggers so that the data remains structurally sound after the commit. Isolation is the promise that concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other; the classic example is that if I'm transferring money while another process is reading the balances, I won't see a dirty read or a partial update. The database typically gives us a choice between serializable isolation, which is the strictest, and read committed, which lets non-repeatable reads happen but is faster. Durability guarantees that once a transaction commits, its effects are permanent, even if the system crashes immediately after. This is usually achieved by writing to a write-ahead log or a redo log before acknowledging the commit, so on restart the database can replay those records and recover the exact state. When transferring money between two accounts, atomicity is the guarantee that prevents the money from being deducted from one account but never credited to the other if the process crashes midway. Because both the debit and the credit are inside one transaction, the database treats them as an all-or-nothing operation. If the system loses power after the debit succeeds but before the credit is applied, the uncommitted transaction is rolled back when the database restarts, restoring both accounts to their pre-transaction balances. The trade-off is that strict atomicity can add latency, since the database must coordinate the two operations and keep a log of the intent; if I were optimizing for write throughput and could tolerate the rare orphaned debit, I might choose a system with eventual consistency or a message queue that retries the credit independently, accepting that some manual reconciliation would be needed after a crash.

The change is first recorded in the log, and the log is flushed with fsync before the commit returns to the client. This means the log record survives an immediate power loss because it's on the device, even though the modified table pages are still sitting in the OS page cache and haven't been written to disk yet. Writing the data pages later is a separate, background operation; it improves throughput but doesn't affect the commit's durability promise. If I turned synchronous commit off, I'd give up that immediate fsync on the log, trading a bounded window - roughly the time between the commit acknowledgment and the next checkpoint or crash - for higher throughput. I'd accept that risk in a development or caching workload where losing a few recent transactions is acceptable, but I'd keep it on for any financial or critical state where even a single lost committed transaction is unacceptable.

It relaxes M to T and sees that 5 plus negative 2 gives 3, which is less than 10, so it updates T's distance to 3 and pushes it onto the queue. The greedy invariant that a settled node's distance is final falls apart because a later negative edge can always undercut a distance already committed to. I would choose the list-and-join approach whenever the pieces are discrete strings; if I were streaming data or the chunks were already byte arrays, I might reach for a StringBuilder or a buffer protocol instead, trading off the slight overhead of an extra container against the quadratic copy cost.

The failure is a cache stampede, and it's a property of the expiry design, not the traffic level. With a 60-second TTL, every reader that misses at exactly the same wall-clock moment will all hammer the database at once. The design guarantees that the key expires at a deterministic time, so under peak load many concurrent requests will observe the same stale value and all decide to recompute it simultaneously. That synchronisation is the root cause - even light traffic would produce a stampede if enough clients happened to hit the miss window at once, but heavy traffic just makes the downstream impact worse. Two mitigations: first, request coalescing under a lock or semaphore so only one thread recomputes and the others wait or reuse its result; that costs added latency for the waiting threads and complexity in the cache library. Second, probabilistic early expiry, where each reader refreshes the key with a small random probability a few seconds before the TTL expires, spreading the recomputation load over time; that costs a small amount of extra cache writes and the risk of briefly serving a newer value than the TTL technically allows. I'd choose coalescing when the recomputation is expensive and idempotent, and early expiry when the workload is bursty and I want to smooth the load without adding locks.

The coordination cost is real: every write incurs extra round-trips to achieve consensus, and under a network partition the system would have to choose between availability and consistency, per the CAP theorem. For the likes counter, the stakes are lower. A user might see a like count that's off by a few seconds, and that's acceptable. Eventual consistency is fine here: replicas will converge to the same value once writes stop, and there's no strict bound on how long that takes unless we explicitly add one. If I demanded strong consistency for both, the cost would be higher tail latency on every like, and the system would become less available during partitions. I'd only choose strong consistency for the likes if the product required real-time leaderboards or fraud detection, but for a standard social feed, the trade-off favors availability and lower latency. I'm unsure about the exact quorum sizes needed if we scaled to thousands of writes per second, but the principle stays the same: balance the risk of stale data against the latency and availability penalties of coordination.

For retries I use exponential backoff with jitter: the delay starts short and doubles each attempt, but a random offset is added so that many clients don't all retry at the same moment, which would otherwise cause a thundering herd and amplify load onto B when it's already struggling. The retry count is capped so that after a few attempts we give up rather than keep hammering a dependency that can't keep up. This matters because a naive retry without backoff or timeout just piles more requests onto B's queue, turning B's slowness into retry_amplification and exhausting A's connection pool, which then cascades into a full outage for A's own users. I'd rather have A shed load early via the timeout budget than keep retrying and risk cascading_failure. The trade-off is latency versus reliability: if B is only intermittently slow a short timeout with few retries might increase error rates for legitimate callers, whereas a longer timeout with aggressive backoff risks keeping A's threads tied up longer. I'm unsure exactly where the right budget lies without load testing, but the principle of bounding wait time and randomising retries is the guardrail I'd start from.

Adding a per-user label destroys that efficiency, so I keep cardinality low. For understanding individual events - why a particular deployment caused a spike, or whether a specific error is recurring - I use logs. Logs have the most detail per event, but they don't aggregate well, so I'm careful not to rely on them for population-level questions. I'm still unsure how to balance trace sampling against cost when traffic is extremely high, but for a single user report, I'd always start with a trace.

Metrics aggregate over time so they answer how many requests per second are flowing well, but they answer which specific request was slow badly because you lose the per-request context the moment you sum. Traces follow one request across services so they answer where the time went for that request well, but they answer how the whole system is behaving badly because a single trace doesn't tell you if the slowdown is widespread. When a single user reports one request was slow I would reach for traces first because they show the exact path and latency of that call, and I would ignore metrics because they would just give me a noisy aggregate that hides the real problem.

So vertical versus horizontal scaling - that's a bigger machine versus more machines. And availability-wise, one machine is one point of failure, however large it is. If that box goes down, you're down, period. That's the trade-off right there - you get more capacity but you lose redundancy. On the horizontal side, you're adding machines, and that buys you capacity but you're paying for coordination, partial failure, and consistency questions. The operational complexity goes up a lot because now you have to think about how data's distributed, how failures propagate, and whether your state's consistent across the cluster. One workload where vertical scaling is genuinely the better engineering decision is a stateful in-memory cache like Redis. If you're doing pure key-value lookups with a small working set, the latency benefits of a single machine with everything in RAM and no network hops between nodes massively outweigh the availability risk. You can mitigate that with replication, but the critical path stays on one node. The limit that eventually forces a horizontal approach is memory capacity - you hit the point where a single machine can't hold your working set, and then you have to shard across multiple boxes anyway. I'm not 100% sure where that break-even point is for every application, but for read-heavy, small-working-set workloads, vertical usually wins until you hit that memory ceiling.

Scaling vertically means buying a bigger machine - more cpus, more memory, faster disks - and running the same process on it. It's simpler to start with because you don't have to change the code, but it comes with an immediate availability problem: one machine is one point of failure. If that box goes down, everything stops, no matter how powerful it is. Scaling horizontally means adding more machines and running multiple instances behind a load balancer. A request might hit one node that has stale data, or a node might die mid-request and you need retries. The trade-off is that you gain resilience - if one node fails, the others keep serving - but you pay for it in engineering overhead. A workload where vertical scaling is genuinely the better decision is a single-threaded, stateful service like a small Redis instance or a local cache that doesn't need high throughput. The limit that eventually forces a horizontal approach is the physical ceiling of a single machine - you can only add so many cpus and memory before you hit diminishing returns and the cost becomes unreasonable, at which point you have to split the load across multiple boxes.

When you scale vertically you are essentially buying a bigger machine, adding more cpu cores or more memory to a single node and that gives you an immediate bump in throughput because the application can just use more resources without having to worry about how data gets split across different endpoints. I have seen this work well for workloads that are inherently single-threaded or have a very tight coupling to a local database where the latency of talking to another machine would actually hurt more than the benefit of adding another box, like a real-time analytics aggregator that processes logs as they come in. I start with access pattern analysis. User profiles are read far more often than they are written, so I would store them in a relational database with an index on the primary key and a secondary index on email. That gives me point lookups in the low single-digit milliseconds and handles the occasional update without rewriting the whole row. The audit trail is append-only, meaning every write is immutable and time-ordered; I would use a columnar store or a specialized append-only log where new events are written sequentially and old segments are compressed or tiered to cheaper storage. For the query workload, range queries over time windows are common, and I need to keep scan costs bounded by compaction policies. Profile images are large immutable blobs, so object storage is the right fit: I store just the URL and metadata in the relational database, and the actual file lives in S3 or a compatible system with lifecycle rules that transition objects to cold storage after 90 days and expire them after a year. The read/write ratio for images is skewed heavily toward read, so I would add a CDN in front of the bucket to cache hot avatars. The trade-off here is complexity versus cost - I could keep images in the relational store using a large binary column, but that would inflate backup sizes and slow restores. I would choose the database-only approach unless the images exceed a few megabytes or the team needs strong transactional consistency between profile data and the image file, in which case I would revisit the split. I am unsure how the audit trail query pattern will evolve if we need ad-hoc filtering on event attributes beyond timestamp, which might push me toward a document store instead of a pure log structure.

For user profiles I'd use a relational database because the access pattern is mostly point lookups by user ID and occasional updates to fields like email or password. The read-to-write ratio is high and the data is relatively small per row, so the transactional guarantees and index lookups are the right fit. For the append-only audit trail I'd choose a log-structured storage engine, something like a columnar file format or a dedicated append-only append-only database. The key is that every write is immutable and time-ordered, and queries are typically range scans over time windows or filtering by event type, so writing to a sequential file and compressing old segments gives us cheap retention and fast range queries without random I/O overhead. For profile images I'd store the binary data in an object store and keep only the metadata and a reference key in the relational database. The access pattern is read-once or occasional re-derivative generation, and the files are large and mostly static after upload, so the economics of object storage with its HTTP access pattern and built-in durability make sense, but the decision is driven entirely by the read-heavy, size-per-item and retention profile, not by the fact that the data is binary.

For user profiles I'd pick a document store because the access pattern is read-heavy with occasional writes and the query shape varies across fields like name, email, and preferences. The read/write ratio is skewed toward reads, so the store needs to serve point lookups fast without paying for transactional overhead I don't use. For the audit trail I'd choose a key-value store with a time-to-live feature, since the workload is append-only and queried by range or prefix - new entries are written once and read in order, and I can set expiration on old chunks to keep costs down. Profile images are best kept in object storage because the access pattern is read-once or streamed display, the files are large and immutable, and attaching a URL to a relational record is the simplest way to reference them without bloating the row. Each choice comes down to how the data moves, not how it's structured.

Okay so when we think about the user profiles themselves we need something that can handle reads by user id and maybe some profile fields like email or display name. A relational database works well there because we can index on the primary key and do equality lookups quickly. The access pattern is basically one user at a time, maybe a few fields updated or read, nothing too fancy. For the audit trail that is append only and gets queried by time ranges, say last 30 days or by user over their lifetime. That really begs for a wide column store or something like Cassandra where you can write sequentially and then scan forward in time without random I/O killing you. And for the uploaded images those are just large binary blobs that are read once and served up to a browser or mobile app. Object storage is the natural fit there, S3 style, where you just store the key and the URL sits in the profile record. That keeps the database lean and lets the blob store handle the heavy lifting of streaming large files. The key thing across all of it is matching the technology to how the data actually gets used rather than what the data looks like on the surface.

For user profiles I'd reach for a document store like MongoDB because the data is naturally hierarchical and you can shard it easily across zones; the read-heavy access pattern means you can index the fields users actually query on and keep the rest in a sparse schema so you're not paying for unused columns. The audit trail is a perfect fit for an append-only log in something like Apache Cassandra - write throughput is the bottleneck there, and Cassandra's distributed write path means you can scale ingest without hitting a single hot partition, plus you get eventual consistency across datacenters for compliance retention. Profile images belong in object storage like S3 because the access pattern is download-once-then-never, and storing the binary blob alongside metadata in a relational database would kill your IOPS; you just keep the key and let the CDN handle the rest. Each choice comes down to whether you're reading a single record, streaming appends, or serving static assets, and that's the only variable that should drive the decision.
